description: Une équipe multidisciplinaire basée à Dakar combinant logiciels, IA, données et agriculture. Pour Field Shift, nous visons à construire un outil d’aide à la décision utilisant les observations terrestres de la NASA et les données agricoles locales afin d’aider les agriculteurs à explorer des stratégies de rotation des cultures résilientes. Nous accueillons les coéquipiers en agronomie, science des sols, télédétection, science des données, IA/ML, UX/UI et communication.
summary:
In Senegal's Niayes region, thousands of market gardeners depend on fruit and vegetable production for their livelihoods. Yet, when deciding what to plant and how to organize their crop rotations, many farmers still rely on experience or what worked during the previous season. They have little access to information showing how their choices might perform under different weather conditions.

We developed SUUF to explore this problem. The tool compares three crop rotation strategies involving onion, cowpea and tomato: the farmer's current practice and two alternative approaches. To do this, we used 25 years of NASA POWER climate data (2001–2025), covering 9,131 days, and applied the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith method to estimate crop water requirements.

Rather than simply presenting technical climate data, SUUF translates the results into simple comparisons, yearly breakdowns and visual explanations that farmers can understand and use. The goal is not to tell farmers what they must grow, but to help them see how different choices could affect their water needs across seasons.

We also recognize that climate data and theoretical estimates have limitations. SUUF makes these uncertainties visible instead of presenting its results as guaranteed predictions.

For us, the value of this project lies in making 25 years of climate information more accessible and useful for the people whose livelihoods depend on agriculture.
details:
What the project does

SUTURA AGRI is a web application that helps market gardeners in Senegal's Niayes region compare different crop rotation strategies using historical climate data.

A farmer can enter their current rotation and compare it with two alternatives involving onion, cowpea and tomato. The idea is simple: instead of relying only on what happened during the previous season, farmers can explore how these different choices would have performed under the region's weather conditions over the past 25 years.

How it works

The application follows a series of steps, from climate data collection to the presentation of results.

1. Defining the rotations

The farmer, or an agricultural adviser working with them, defines three rotation strategies:

  • Rotation A: current farming practice.
  • Rotation B: first alternative.
  • Rotation C: second alternative.

2. Collecting climate data

We use daily climate records from NASA POWER for Mboro, in the Niayes region, covering 2001 to 2025. The dataset contains 9,131 days and includes temperature, humidity, wind speed, solar radiation, dewpoint and rainfall.

3. Estimating crop water requirements

The scientific engine calculates reference evapotranspiration (ET0) using the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith method.

We checked our implementation against a worked example published by FAO, with a difference of less than 0.1%.

Crop water requirements (ETc) are then estimated using crop coefficients (Kc) corresponding to the different growth stages of onion, cowpea and tomato. We use FAO-56 reference tables and local technical documents where available.

Not all coefficients have been confirmed for local growing conditions. We therefore distinguish documented values from theoretical assumptions and keep their sources visible.

4. Comparing 25 years of climate history

Each rotation is evaluated against the climate conditions of every year in the dataset.

We present two measurements:

  • Total theoretical water requirement over the growing cycle.
  • Average daily water requirement.

We decided to keep both because they do not always tell the same story. A rotation may require less water overall but more water per cultivation day. Showing only one measurement could give a misleading impression.

5. Handling uncertain data

Some rainfall records, particularly for 2019 and 2020, require further verification. These years are marked as under verification in the application.

We do not silently treat uncertain information as confirmed data.

6. Making the results accessible

The interface was designed with smallholder farmers in mind, including people who may have difficulty reading technical information.

We chose to use:

  • Pictures and pictograms before long text.
  • One main decision per screen.
  • Visual water indicators alongside numerical results.
  • Simple comparisons rather than scientific tables.
  • Both shapes and colors to communicate information, so users do not have to rely on color alone.

The intention is to make the application understandable without requiring users to have a technical background.

Benefits

SUTURA AGRI gives farmers and agricultural advisers another way to think about crop rotation decisions.

Instead of comparing strategies based only on personal experience or the previous harvest, they can examine how each option relates to 25 years of recorded climate conditions.

It also makes the assumptions behind the calculations visible. Users can distinguish between confirmed information, theoretical estimates and data that still needs verification.

Expected impact

The Niayes region is one of Senegal's main vegetable-producing areas. Agricultural production there is increasingly affected by irregular rainfall and pressure on water resources.

We hope SUTURA AGRI can contribute to better-informed agricultural decisions, particularly when farmers need to consider the water requirements of different crop sequences.

Our ambition is to make climate information more useful at the local level, while keeping farmers' experience and knowledge at the center of the decision-making process.

What makes the project different

One of our main design choices was not to reduce the results to a single score or automatically declare one rotation the best.

During development, we realized that two strategies could produce different results depending on whether we looked at total water requirements or daily water requirements.

We therefore decided to show both.

We also chose to display uncertain coefficients and questionable climate records instead of hiding them. This makes the results less simplistic, but more transparent.

For us, a useful agricultural tool should not only provide an answer. It should also show where that answer comes from and what its limitations are.

Factors we considered

Several considerations guided our development:

  • Local relevance: focusing on crops actually grown in the Niayes region, particularly onion, cowpea and tomato.
  • Accessibility: designing an interface that does not depend on users being comfortable with reading or technical terminology.
  • Scientific reliability: using an established FAO methodology and checking the implementation against a published reference example.
  • Data traceability: documenting the origin and status of the parameters used in the calculations.
  • Transparency: distinguishing measured climate data, documented parameters and theoretical assumptions.
  • Responsible interpretation: avoiding invented thresholds, unsupported resilience scores or claims about future agricultural yields.

Current limitations and future improvements

SUTURA AGRI is currently a prototype focused on Mboro and three crops.

Some crop coefficients and growth-stage durations are based on FAO-56 reference tables because locally validated technical information was not available for every parameter. These values still need field validation.

Effective rainfall and irrigation efficiency are also represented by documented assumptions rather than direct field measurements.

The 2019–2020 rainfall records require independent verification, for example through comparison with GPM IMERG data.

Another limitation concerns the spatial resolution of NASA POWER. Its climate data represent an approximately 55 × 62 km grid cell, not the exact conditions of an individual farm plot.

Finally, the application estimates theoretical crop water requirements. It does not predict crop yields, soil fertility or overall farm resilience.

Our next steps are to work with local agricultural institutions such as ISRA-CDH and ANCAR to validate crop parameters, investigate the questionable rainfall records and gradually extend the tool to other communes and crops in the Niayes region.

Technologies and tools

The project was developed using:

  • Python: scientific calculations and backend development.
  • FastAPI: backend API.
  • Next.js: web application framework.
  • React: user interface.
  • TypeScript: frontend development.
  • NASA POWER API: historical climate data.
  • FAO-56 Penman-Monteith: reference evapotranspiration methodology.
  • pytest: automated testing of the scientific calculations.
